visual.caption: Both books describe one account, written from opposite sides.

slides.narration: Welcome to the chapter on the bank reconciliation statement. A firm keeps a cash book, and its bank keeps a pass book. Both describe the same account, yet on the same day they seldom show the same balance. In this part we see why the books differ, why that matters, and which causes are timing differences and which are errors.

slides.heading: Pass book and cash book
slides.body_md: The **pass book** (bank statement) is the bank's copy of the customer's account. The bank column of the **cash book** is the firm's copy.

visual.alt: Table comparing the cash book and the pass book: who keeps each, how a deposit, a payment, a favourable balance and an overdraft appear in each

slides.narration: The pass book, also called the bank statement, is the bank's own copy of the customer's account. The cash book is the firm's record, and its bank column describes the same account. The bank and the firm stand on opposite sides, so each transaction is entered on opposite sides. A deposit is a debit in the cash book and a credit in the pass book.

slides.heading: Favourable balance and overdraft
slides.body_md: A **favourable balance** is money at the bank: a debit in the cash book, a credit in the pass book. An **overdraft** is the reverse.

visual.alt: Table comparing the cash book and the pass book: who keeps each, how a deposit, a payment, a favourable balance and an overdraft appear in each

slides.narration: Money at the bank is a favourable balance. In the cash book it is a debit balance, and in the pass book it is a credit balance. An overdraft is the reverse, because the firm has drawn more than it deposited. In the cash book an overdraft is a credit balance, and in the pass book it is a debit balance. Keep this mirror in mind through the whole chapter.

slides.heading: Quick check: reading the balances
slides.body_md: A favourable balance in the two books.
slides.narration: Think of the firm and the bank as opposite parties. Which side does a favourable balance take in the firm cash book, and which side does the bank give it in the pass book? Choose the option that treats the two books as mirror images.

slides.heading: The bank reconciliation statement
slides.body_md: A **bank reconciliation statement** is prepared on a given date to explain the difference between the balance of the cash book and that of the pass book. It is **not an account**.

rows: A statement prepared on a date
An account with debit and credit sides
Explain the difference between two balances

visual.alt: Table comparing a bank reconciliation statement and a bank account: what each is, whether it is part of double entry and its purpose

slides.narration: A bank reconciliation statement is prepared on a chosen date to show why the cash book balance and the pass book balance differ, and to bring them into agreement. It is a statement and not an account. It has no debit and credit sides, it is not part of double entry, and nothing is posted from it to the ledger.

slides.heading: Why prepare the statement

rows: Find the reasons for the difference
Every item that separates the two balances is listed
A difference that cannot be explained points to a mistake or misuse
Items the bank has recorded first show what to enter
A wrong debit or credit by the bank is found

visual.alt: Table of four needs of a bank reconciliation statement: finding reasons, detecting errors and frauds, updating the cash book and checking the bank

slides.narration: There are four reasons to prepare the statement. It finds the reasons for the difference between the two balances. It helps to detect errors and frauds, because a difference that cannot be explained points to a mistake or misuse. It shows which entries must be made to bring the cash book up to date. And it checks the work of the bank.

visual.caption: Timing differences correct themselves; errors must be corrected.

slides.narration: The differences fall into two groups. Timing differences arise when one book records a transaction later than the other. Some are recorded by the firm first, such as cheques issued or deposited. Others are recorded by the bank first, such as charges and interest. Errors are mistakes, either in the cash book or by the bank. Timing differences correct themselves, but errors must be corrected.

slides.heading: Recorded by the firm first
slides.body_md: The firm enters a cheque on the day it issues or deposits it; the bank does so only on **presentation** or **collection**.

headers: Pass book compared with cash book
Entry needed in the cash book
rows: Cheques issued but not yet presented for payment
None: already in the cash book
Cheques deposited but not yet collected (credited by the bank)
None: already in the cash book

visual.alt: Table of causes recorded by the firm first: cheques issued but not yet presented, and cheques deposited but not yet collected, with the effect on the pass book and the entry needed in the cash book

slides.narration: Two causes are recorded by the firm first. When the firm issues a cheque it credits the bank column at once, but the bank pays only when the supplier presents the cheque, so the pass book is higher until then. When the firm deposits a cheque it debits the bank column at once, but the bank credits it after collection, so the pass book is lower. No entry is needed in the cash book.

slides.heading: Quick check: timing or error
slides.body_md: Which item is a timing difference?
slides.narration: A timing difference is a transaction that both books will record, one of them a little later. A mistake in an amount or in an addition is an error. Read the four items and pick the one that will correct itself when the bank records it.

slides.heading: Recorded by the bank first
slides.body_md: The bank enters charges, interest, collections and payments when they happen; the firm learns of them from the pass book.

headers: Pass book compared with cash book
Entry needed in the cash book
rows: Bank charges debited by the bank
Interest on overdraft debited by the bank
Direct deposit by a customer into the bank
Direct payment by the bank on standing instruction
Dividend or interest collected by the bank

visual.alt: Table of causes recorded by the bank first: charges, interest on overdraft, interest allowed, direct deposit, payment on standing instruction and collection, with the effect on the pass book and the entry needed in the cash book

slides.narration: Other causes are recorded by the bank first. Interest allowed, a direct deposit by a customer and a dividend collected by the bank all increase the pass book. Bank charges, interest on overdraft and a payment under a standing instruction decrease it. The firm must enter each of these in its cash book, a receipt on the debit side and a payment on the credit side of the bank column.

slides.heading: A dishonoured cheque
slides.body_md: A cheque deposited and returned unpaid is first counted by the firm and then reversed by the bank.

rows: Credit the bank column; debit the customer

visual.alt: Table of the steps of a dishonoured cheque in the cash book and the pass book

slides.narration: A cheque that the firm has deposited may be returned unpaid. The firm has already debited the bank column, and the bank, after the return, debits the account. Until the firm learns of it, the pass book is lower than the cash book. When the firm learns of it, it credits the bank column and debits the customer, so that the debt of the customer is revived.

slides.narration: Neel Traders, an imagined firm, finds eight differences on thirtieth April. The two cheques were recorded by the firm first, so no cash book entry is needed. The other six were recorded by the bank first. Interest, the direct deposit and the dividend are receipts, so they are debits in the bank column. Charges, the rent and the returned cheque are payments, so they are credits.

bullets: Each of the six causes moves the pass book relative to the cash book.

visual.alt: Table of the six causes that make the pass book balance 64,560 differ from the cash book balance 62,500: the net difference is 2,060 rupees

slides.narration: Neel Traders had eleven transactions in March. Its cash book shows rupees sixty two thousand five hundred, and the pass book of Sagar Bank shows rupees sixty four thousand five hundred sixty. The pass book is higher by rupees two thousand sixty. The six causes explain every rupee of this gap: cheques issued raise the pass book, cheques deposited lower it, and each bank item raises or lowers it by its own amount.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: timing against bank items
slides.body_md: Of the ₹2,060 difference, the cheques account for **₹3,500** and the bank items for **−₹1,440**.

**Pass book balance less cash book balance**

slides.narration: The difference of rupees two thousand sixty can be split in two parts. The two kinds of cheque together make the pass book higher by rupees three thousand five hundred. The items that the bank recorded first make it lower by rupees one thousand four hundred forty. The first part needs no cash book entry. The second part tells the firm which entries it must still make.

slides.heading: Quick check: the size of the difference
slides.body_md: Three differences, one number.
slides.narration: Find by how much the pass book is higher than the cash book. Cheques issued but not presented make the pass book higher, cheques deposited but not collected make it lower, and the bank charges make it lower. Combine the three effects with their signs.

slides.heading: Errors in either book

rows: Receipt entered too low or a debit side added short
Payment entered too low or a credit side added short
Deposit credited to the wrong customer

visual.alt: Table of errors in the cash book and by the bank, who made each, the effect on the balance and who puts it right

slides.narration: Errors are different from timing differences. The firm may enter a receipt too low or add a side short, which makes the cash book wrong. The bank may credit a deposit to the wrong customer or debit a cheque of another customer, which makes the pass book wrong. The firm corrects its own book. A bank error stays in the statement until the bank puts it right.

slides.heading: Quick check: match the terms
slides.body_md: Terms and meanings.
slides.narration: Match each term with its meaning. The pass book belongs to the bank and the cash book to the firm. An overdraft is the reverse of a favourable balance, and the reconciliation statement explains the gap between the two balances on a date.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1
bullets: The cash book and the pass book are mirror images of one account.
The statement is prepared on a date to explain the difference; it is not an account.
Timing differences: recorded by the firm first, or by the bank first. Errors: in the cash book or by the bank.

rows: Cash book (firm) and pass book (bank) are mirror images; a favourable balance is a debit in one and a credit in the other
Prepared on a date to explain the difference; not an account
Reasons, errors and frauds, updating the cash book, checking the bank

visual.alt: Summary table of the two books, the reconciliation statement, its need and the causes of difference

slides.narration: To sum up. The cash book and the pass book are mirror images of one account. The reconciliation statement explains the difference between their balances on a date, and it is not an account. Differences are timing differences, recorded first by the firm or by the bank, or errors, made in the cash book or by the bank. In the next part we prepare the statement.

slides.narration: In the examination, say which book recorded each item first, because that decides whether a cash book entry is needed. Keep timing differences and errors apart. Remember that a deposit is a debit in the cash book and a credit in the pass book. And for every item recorded by the bank first, name the side of the bank column on which the firm should enter it.

sections.heading: 1. Two books, one bank account
sections.body_md:
A firm that banks with a bank has two records of one account. The **cash book** (bank column) is kept by the firm; the **pass book** (bank statement) is the bank's copy of the customer's account. Because the firm and the bank are opposite parties, a transaction appears on opposite sides: a **deposit** is a **debit** in the cash book and a **credit** in the pass book; a payment or withdrawal is a credit in the cash book and a debit in the pass book.

A **favourable balance** (money at the bank) is a debit balance in the cash book and a credit balance in the pass book. An **overdraft** is a credit balance in the cash book and a debit balance in the pass book.

key_terms.definition_md: The bank's copy of a customer's account, showing deposits, withdrawals and the balance.
Money held at the bank: a debit balance in the cash book and a credit balance in the pass book.
The amount by which the firm has drawn more than it deposited: a credit balance in the cash book and a debit balance in the pass book.

sections.heading: 2. Bank reconciliation statement: meaning and need
sections.body_md:
A **bank reconciliation statement** is a statement prepared on a given date to reconcile the balance of the cash book with that of the pass book. It is **not an account**: it has no debit and credit sides and nothing is posted from it.

Its **needs** are to find the reasons for the difference, to detect errors and frauds, to show the entries needed to update the cash book, and to check the work of the bank.

key_terms.definition_md: A statement prepared on a date to explain the difference between the cash book balance and the pass book balance and bring them into agreement.
The differences listed in the statement, each of which is added or deducted.

sections.heading: 3. Causes of difference: timing differences and errors
sections.body_md:
A **timing difference** arises when one book records a transaction in one period and the other book in a later one; it corrects itself. Two groups: (a) **recorded by the firm first**: cheques issued but not yet presented for payment; cheques deposited but not yet collected (credited); (b) **recorded by the bank first**: bank charges and interest on overdraft; interest allowed; direct deposits by customers; direct payments by the bank on standing instruction; dividends or interest collected by the bank; cheques deposited and dishonoured. Group (b) needs an entry in the cash book: receipts on the debit side and payments on the credit side of the bank column.

**Errors** are mistakes in the cash book (a wrong amount, a wrong addition, an item left out) or by the bank (a wrong credit or debit). They do not correct themselves.

key_terms.definition_md: A difference caused by one book recording a transaction later than the other; it disappears when the other book records it.
A cheque recorded by the firm when issued, but not yet paid by the bank.
A cheque recorded by the firm when deposited, but not yet credited by the bank.
An order to the bank to make a regular payment, such as an insurance premium, from the account.
A deposited cheque that the bank returns unpaid; the bank debits the account and the firm credits the bank column and debits the customer.

sections.heading: 4. Preparing the statement: the rule
sections.body_md:
Steps: note the starting balance (favourable or overdraft); list every difference; decide to **add or deduct** each; work out the result; check it against the other book.

One question decides the sign: **does the item make the other book show a higher favourable balance?** From a favourable balance: add if yes, deduct if no. From an overdraft the treatment is reversed. Starting from the pass book reverses every treatment used from the cash book. A negative result is reported as an **overdraft**.

key_terms.definition_md: An item that makes the other book higher is added to a favourable starting balance.
With an overdraft as the starting balance, an item that makes the other book show a larger overdraft is added and one that makes it smaller is deducted.

sections.heading: 6. Amended cash book and the statement that follows
sections.body_md:
An **amended (adjusted) cash book** brings the cash book up to date for items the bank has recorded and the firm has not: interest allowed, dividends collected and direct deposits on the debit side; charges, interest on overdraft, payments on standing instruction and dishonoured cheques on the credit side. For Neel Traders: ₹62,500 becomes ₹61,060.

The statement then starts from the amended balance and shows only the **cheque timing differences** (and any bank error): add ₹17,500, deduct ₹14,000, reach ₹64,560. A cash book error is corrected in the cash book; a bank error stays in the statement until the bank corrects it.

notes.exam_tips_md:
- Say which book recorded the item **first**: it decides whether a cash book entry is needed.
- Keep **timing differences** and **errors** apart.
- Ask: does the item make the other book **higher**? Favourable start: add if yes; overdraft start: reversed.
- Starting from the pass book reverses every treatment.
- Write the heading (firm and date), name the starting balance, and check the result against the other book.
- A negative result is an **overdraft**. If asked for an amended cash book, show it as a ledger account before the statement.

cards.front_md: **Pass book** (bank statement)
cards.back_md: The bank's copy of a customer's account.

cards.front_md: **Cash book** (bank column) and the pass book
cards.back_md: Two records of one account, written from opposite sides.

cards.front_md: A deposit in the two books
cards.back_md: Debit in the cash book; credit in the pass book.

cards.front_md: A withdrawal or payment in the two books
cards.back_md: Credit in the cash book; debit in the pass book.

cards.front_md: **Favourable balance**
cards.back_md: Money at the bank: a debit balance in the cash book, a credit balance in the pass book.

cards.front_md: **Overdraft**
cards.back_md: A credit balance in the cash book and a debit balance in the pass book.

cards.front_md: **Bank reconciliation statement**
cards.back_md: A statement prepared on a date to explain the difference between the cash book balance and the pass book balance.

cards.front_md: Is a reconciliation statement an account?
cards.back_md: No. It is a statement; it has no debit and credit sides and nothing is posted from it.

cards.front_md: Needs of a reconciliation statement
cards.back_md: Find the reasons for the difference; detect errors and frauds; update the cash book; check the bank.

cards.front_md: **Timing difference**
cards.back_md: A difference because one book records a transaction later than the other; it corrects itself.

cards.front_md: Two groups of timing differences
cards.back_md: Recorded by the firm first; recorded by the bank first.

cards.front_md: Cheque issued but not yet presented
cards.back_md: In the cash book only; pass book higher; no cash book entry needed.

cards.front_md: Cheque deposited but not yet collected
cards.back_md: In the cash book only; pass book lower; no cash book entry needed.

cards.front_md: Bank charges not in the cash book
cards.back_md: Pass book lower; credit the bank column.

cards.front_md: Interest allowed by the bank, not in the cash book
cards.back_md: Pass book higher; debit the bank column.

cards.front_md: Interest on overdraft debited by the bank
cards.back_md: Pass book lower; credit the bank column.

cards.front_md: Direct deposit by a customer
cards.back_md: Pass book higher; debit the bank column.

cards.front_md: Payment by the bank on **standing instruction**
cards.back_md: Pass book lower; credit the bank column.

cards.front_md: Dividend or interest collected by the bank
cards.back_md: Pass book higher; debit the bank column.

cards.front_md: **Dishonoured cheque**
cards.back_md: Returned unpaid and debited by the bank; the firm credits the bank column and debits the customer.

cards.front_md: Errors that cause a difference
cards.back_md: Mistakes in the cash book (wrong amount, wrong addition, item left out) or by the bank (wrong credit or debit).

cards.front_md: Steps of preparing the statement
cards.back_md: Note the starting balance; list the differences; decide add or deduct; work out the result; check it.

cards.front_md: The question that decides add or deduct
cards.back_md: Does the item make the other book show a higher favourable balance?

cards.front_md: Favourable cash book start: cheques issued not presented
cards.back_md: Add.

cards.front_md: Favourable cash book start: cheques deposited not collected
cards.back_md: Deduct.

cards.front_md: Starting from the pass book instead of the cash book
cards.back_md: Every treatment is reversed; the result is the cash book balance.

cards.front_md: Starting from an overdraft
cards.back_md: The add or deduct treatment of a favourable balance is reversed.

cards.front_md: A negative result in the statement
cards.back_md: It is an overdraft, not a favourable balance.

cards.front_md: **Amended cash book**
cards.back_md: The cash book brought up to date for items the bank recorded first, so that only cheque timing differences remain.

cards.front_md: After amending the cash book, what remains in the statement?
cards.back_md: Cheques issued but not presented and cheques deposited but not collected, and any bank error.

cards.front_md: Where is a bank error corrected?
cards.back_md: By the bank. Until then it stays in the statement; the firm makes no cash book entry.

questions.stem_md: Every month Sagar Bank sends Neel Traders, an imagined firm, a copy of the firm's current account as the bank has recorded it. This copy is called the

options.text_md: cash book
pass book (bank statement)
bank reconciliation statement
trial balance

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** pass book (bank statement). The bank keeps this copy, in which every deposit and withdrawal of the customer is recorded. The cash book is the record of the firm itself, the reconciliation statement is prepared by the firm to compare the two, and a trial balance lists ledger balances.

questions.stem_md: Neel Traders has money at Sagar Bank on 30 September 2026. How does this favourable balance appear in the two books?

options.text_md: A credit balance in the bank column of the cash book and a debit balance in the pass book
A debit balance in both books
A credit balance in both books
A debit balance in the bank column of the cash book and a credit balance in the pass book

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** A debit balance in the bank column of the cash book and a credit balance in the pass book. The firm treats the bank as a receiver of its money, so a favourable balance is a debit in the cash book. The bank owes that money to the firm, so in the bank's own books, and therefore in the pass book, it is a credit. The two books are mirror images.

questions.stem_md: On 12 May 2026 Neel Traders deposited a customer's cheque in its account. The firm entered it on the debit side of the bank column of the cash book. Sagar Bank will show the same deposit in the pass book on the

options.text_md: credit side, because the bank now owes the money to the customer
debit side, because the bank has received money
debit side, as a contra entry
credit side, but only when the firm's cash book agrees

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** credit side, because the bank now owes the money to the customer. A deposit increases what the bank owes the customer, so the bank credits the customer's account. This is why the same transaction is a debit in the cash book and a credit in the pass book. It is not a contra entry, and the bank does not wait for the firm's books.

questions.stem_md: Neel Traders has overdrawn its account with Sagar Bank. In which form will the overdraft appear in the cash book and in the pass book?

options.text_md: A debit balance in the cash book and a credit balance in the pass book
A credit balance in both books
A credit balance in the cash book and a debit balance in the pass book
A debit balance in both books

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** A credit balance in the cash book and a debit balance in the pass book. An overdraft is the reverse of a favourable balance. In the firm's cash book it is a credit balance, and in the bank's record of the firm's account it is a debit balance, because the bank is owed the money.

questions.stem_md: A bank reconciliation statement is best described as

options.text_md: an account in the ledger in which the bank is debited and credited
a book of original entry for cheques
a statement prepared on a given date to show why the balances of the cash book and the pass book differ and to bring them into agreement
a statement issued by the bank every month

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** a statement prepared on a given date to show why the balances of the cash book and the pass book differ and to bring them into agreement. It is a statement prepared by the firm, not by the bank, and it is not an account, so it has no debit and credit sides in the ledger and does not form part of double entry. Its purpose is to explain the difference between the two balances on a date.

questions.stem_md: Which of the following is NOT a purpose of preparing a bank reconciliation statement?

options.text_md: To increase the balance that the bank holds for the firm
To find the reasons for the difference between the two balances
To help detect errors and frauds in either book
To show which items must be entered in the cash book to bring it up to date

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** To increase the balance that the bank holds for the firm. The statement only explains and reconciles balances; it cannot change the money at the bank. The other three are real uses: finding the reasons, detecting errors and frauds, and showing the entries the cash book still needs.

questions.stem_md: While comparing its books on 31 March 2027, Neel Traders finds that a receipt of ₹4,500 was entered in the bank column of the cash book as ₹5,400. This difference is

options.text_md: a timing difference that will disappear when the bank credits the cheque
a bank item that is shown in the statement but needs no entry
a contra entry
an error in the cash book, and it is corrected by an entry in the cash book

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** an error in the cash book, and it is corrected by an entry in the cash book. The firm itself recorded the wrong figure, so this is an error, not a delay. It is put right by correcting the cash book. A timing difference disappears by itself when the other book records the item, and a bank item is something the bank has recorded first.

questions.stem_md: Neel Traders issued a cheque of ₹6,800 to a supplier on 29 October 2026 and entered it in the cash book at once. The supplier presented it at Sagar Bank on 4 November. On 31 October the pass book balance is

options.text_md: lower than the cash book balance by ₹6,800, because the bank has already paid the cheque
higher than the cash book balance by ₹6,800, because the bank has not yet paid the cheque
equal to the cash book balance
higher than the cash book balance by ₹6,800, because the bank has paid the cheque twice

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** higher than the cash book balance by ₹6,800, because the bank has not yet paid the cheque. The firm reduced its cash book balance on the day it issued the cheque, but the bank reduces the pass book balance only when the cheque is presented. Until then the pass book shows the larger figure.

questions.stem_md: Neel Traders deposited a cheque of ₹9,500 on 30 November 2026 and debited the bank column at once; Sagar Bank credited it on 3 December after collection. On 30 November, because of this cheque alone, the

options.text_md: cash book balance is higher than the pass book balance by ₹9,500
cash book balance is lower than the pass book balance by ₹9,500
two balances are the same
pass book balance is an overdraft

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** cash book balance is higher than the pass book balance by ₹9,500. The firm recorded the receipt on the day it deposited the cheque; the bank recorded it only after collection. The cash book therefore runs ahead by the cheque amount until the bank credits it.

questions.stem_md: Sagar Bank debited bank charges of ₹320 to the account of Neel Traders on 31 December 2026. When the firm learns of it from the pass book, it will enter the charges in the cash book on the

options.text_md: debit side of the bank column
credit side of the bank column
credit side of the cash column
debit side of the cash column

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** credit side of the bank column. Bank charges reduce the money at the bank, so they are a payment and go on the credit side of the bank column. The cash column is not affected.

questions.stem_md: Neel Traders deposited a cheque of ₹12,000 from Gopal Rao on 26 February 2027 and entered it in the cash book. On 28 February Sagar Bank returned it unpaid and debited the account. The firm has not yet heard of this. Compared with the cash book, the pass book balance is

options.text_md: higher by ₹12,000, and the firm must debit the bank column
lower by ₹12,000, and no entry is needed in the cash book
lower by ₹12,000, and the firm must credit the bank column and debit Gopal Rao
the same, because the cheque was deposited in both books

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** lower by ₹12,000, and the firm must credit the bank column and debit Gopal Rao. The bank has reversed the deposit, so the pass book falls while the cash book still shows the receipt. The firm must then credit the bank column and debit the customer, whose debt revives. The second option has the direction wrong, the third wrongly says no entry is needed, and the fourth ignores the reversal.

questions.stem_md: On 20 January 2027 Sunita Agencies paid ₹7,200 directly into the account of Neel Traders at Sagar Bank, and the firm learnt of it only from the pass book. In the cash book the entry is made on the

options.text_md: credit side of the bank column
debit side of the cash column
credit side of the cash column
debit side of the bank column

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** debit side of the bank column. A direct deposit increases the money at the bank, so it is a receipt and a debit in the bank column. It is not a cash receipt, so the cash column is not used.

questions.stem_md: Under a standing instruction, Sagar Bank paid an insurance premium of ₹3,600 for Neel Traders on 15 February 2027. Before the firm records it in the cash book, the

options.text_md: pass book balance is higher than the cash book balance by ₹3,600
cash book balance is already lower by ₹3,600
two balances still agree
pass book balance is lower than the cash book balance by ₹3,600

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** pass book balance is lower than the cash book balance by ₹3,600. The bank has paid out money, so the pass book has fallen. Until the firm credits the bank column for the premium, its cash book balance is higher than the pass book balance by the premium.

questions.stem_md: Sagar Bank collected a dividend of ₹2,000 on shares held by Neel Traders and credited it to the firm's account. The pass book shows it, but the cash book does not yet. Which statement is correct?

options.text_md: The firm should credit the bank column; until then the cash book balance is the higher one
No entry is needed, because the bank is responsible for it
The firm should debit the bank column; until then the pass book balance is the higher one
The item should be shown only in the bank's books

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** The firm should debit the bank column; until then the pass book balance is the higher one. The bank has added money to the account, so the firm records a receipt in the bank column. Until it does, its cash book balance is the lower one. The bank's collection is a service for the firm and must be entered in the firm's own books.

questions.stem_md: Neel Traders' accountant sorts the differences found on 30 June 2026 into timing differences and errors. Which one is a timing difference?

options.text_md: A payment of ₹8,300 written in the cash book as ₹3,800
A cheque issued on 29 June and presented by the supplier on 2 July
A deposit of ₹5,000 credited by the bank to the wrong customer
The debit side of the bank column added short by ₹1,000

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** A cheque issued on 29 June and presented by the supplier on 2 July. Only the cheque is a transaction that both books will record, one of them a little later. The other three are mistakes that will not correct themselves. The last is a mistake of the firm's clerk and the third is a mistake of the bank.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A bank reconciliation statement is not an account in the ledger.

**Reason (R):** It is only a statement prepared on a date to reconcile two balances, and it has no debit and credit sides for double entry.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true, and R is the reason for A. The statement lists items to explain a difference; nothing is posted from it, so it is outside the double entry system.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Neel Traders makes no entry in its cash book for cheques issued but not yet presented at the bank.

**Reason (R):** Such cheques were entered in the cash book on the day they were issued.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both statements are true and R explains A. The firm has already recorded the cheque; only the bank has yet to record it, so nothing more is entered in the cash book.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A difference between the cash book and the pass book can arise even when no cheque is outstanding.

**Reason (R):** The cash book is written by the firm and the pass book is written by the bank.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Both are true. Bank charges, direct deposits and interest are recorded by the bank first, which causes a difference without any outstanding cheque. R is also true, but who keeps each book does not by itself explain why a difference remains when no cheque is outstanding.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Because of a cheque issued but not yet presented, the pass book balance is lower than the cash book balance.

**Reason (R):** The bank has not yet debited the cheque to the account of the firm.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** A is false: the bank has not yet reduced its figure, so the pass book balance is higher. R is true, and it is exactly why A fails.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** When interest allowed by the bank is entered in the cash book, the balance of the cash book rises.

**Reason (R):** Interest allowed by the bank is entered on the credit side of the bank column of the cash book.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** A is true because the interest is a receipt. R is false: it is entered on the debit side of the bank column, which is the side that raises a favourable balance.

questions.stem_md: A bank reconciliation statement is posted to the ledger as the bank account.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** It is a statement prepared for a given date, not an account. Nothing is posted from it. Only the items that need an entry in the cash book are entered there.

questions.stem_md: An overdraft on the account of a firm appears as a debit balance in its pass book.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **True.** The bank has lent the firm money and is owed it, so the bank debits the account. In the firm's cash book the same overdraft is a credit balance.

questions.stem_md: A favourable balance is a ___ balance in the cash book and a ___ balance in the pass book.
questions.solution_md: The firm debits the bank column for deposits and the bank credits the customer's account for them, so a favourable balance is a debit in the cash book and a credit in the pass book.

questions.stem_md: Cheques ___ but not yet presented for payment make the pass book balance ___ than the cash book balance, when the balance is favourable.
questions.solution_md: The firm has already deducted the cheques that it issued, while the bank has not, so the bank's figure is higher.

questions.stem_md: Match each bank-reconciliation term in column A with what it means for the cash book or passbook in column B.

options.text_md: Pass book
Cash book
Overdraft
Bank reconciliation statement

match_right.text_md: The firm's own record of receipts and payments including the bank column
A statement that explains the difference between the two balances on a date
The bank's record of a customer's account
A credit balance in the cash book and a debit balance in the pass book

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(r), (b)–(p), (c)–(s), (d)–(q). The pass book belongs to the bank, the cash book to the firm. An overdraft is the reverse of a favourable balance, and the reconciliation statement explains the gap.

questions.stem_md: Match each cause of difference in column A with its effect in column B, for a firm with a favourable balance.

options.text_md: Cheque issued, not yet presented
Interest allowed by the bank
Bank charges
Cheque deposited, not yet collected

match_right.text_md: Pass book balance is lower; no entry needed in the cash book
Pass book balance is higher; no entry needed in the cash book
Pass book balance is lower; credit the bank column in the cash book
Pass book balance is higher; debit the bank column in the cash book

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(q), (b)–(s), (c)–(r), (d)–(p). Items recorded by the firm only (the two cheques) need no cash book entry, and the pass book is higher for the issued cheque and lower for the deposited one. Items recorded by the bank only need a cash book entry, and the interest raises the balance while the charges lower it.

questions.stem_md: Arrange in order the events that make a cheque issued by Neel Traders appear as an outstanding item on a reconciliation date.

options.text_md: The bank pays the cheque later and debits the account in the pass book
The cheque reaches the supplier, who takes time to bring it to the bank
The reconciliation date arrives before the cheque has been presented
The firm issues the cheque and credits the bank column of the cash book

questions.solution_md: **Correct order:** (d) → (b) → (c) → (a). The cheque is recorded by the firm first, travels to the payee, is still unpresented on the reconciliation date, and is recorded by the bank only afterwards.

marking_scheme.step: Complete correct sequence (all items in place)

questions.stem_md: Neel Traders issued five cheques in June 2026: no. 4411 to Anand Paper for ₹7,400, no. 4412 to Bimal Oils for ₹5,600, no. 4413 to Chandra Hardware for ₹3,250, no. 4414 to Dilip Foods for ₹8,150 and no. 4415 to Esha Dyes for ₹2,700. Sagar Bank's pass book up to 30 June shows only nos. 4411 and 4413 as paid. Find the total of the cheques issued but not yet presented on 30 June (in ₹).

questions.stem_md: On 31 July 2026 Neel Traders found three differences between its books: cheques of ₹8,000 issued but not yet presented, a cheque of ₹3,000 deposited but not yet collected, and bank charges of ₹150 not yet entered in the cash book. By how many rupees is the pass book balance higher than the cash book balance (both balances are favourable)?
questions.solution_md: Pass book − cash book = 8,000 (issued, not presented) − 3,000 (deposited, not collected) − 150 (bank charges) = ₹4,850.

questions.stem_md: Neel Traders and Sagar Bank both showed ₹24,000 in favour of the firm on 1 September 2026. During September the firm deposited a cheque of ₹15,000 from Amar Joshi, which the bank collected; it issued a cheque of ₹11,000 to Bhola Brothers, which the bank paid; and it issued a cheque of ₹4,200 to Chetan Dyes, which was not presented before 30 September. The bank also debited charges of ₹175 that the firm has not yet recorded. Find the balance shown by the pass book on 30 September (in ₹).
questions.solution_md: Pass book: 24,000 + 15,000 − 11,000 − 175 = ₹27,825. The cheque to Chetan Dyes is not yet in the pass book (the cash book balance is ₹23,800).

questions.stem_md: Define the pass book and say how a deposit appears in it compared with the cash book.
questions.solution_md: Definition and the mirror treatment of a deposit.

answer.model_answer_md: The pass book (bank statement) is the bank's copy of a customer's account. A deposit is a debit in the bank column of the cash book but a credit in the pass book, because the bank owes the money to the customer.

marking_scheme.step: Pass book defined as the bank's copy of the customer's account
Deposit: debit in the cash book, credit in the pass book

questions.stem_md: Why does Neel Traders, an imagined firm, prepare a bank reconciliation statement every month? Give two reasons.
questions.solution_md: Any two of: reasons for the difference, detection of errors and frauds, updating the cash book, checking the bank.

answer.model_answer_md: It shows why the cash book and the pass book balances differ and what each difference is. It also helps to find errors or frauds in either book and shows the entries needed to update the cash book.

questions.stem_md: A student says that the bank reconciliation statement of Neel Traders should be posted to the ledger. Explain why this is wrong.
questions.solution_md: It is a statement, not an account.

answer.model_answer_md: The statement is not an account but a statement prepared on a date to explain the difference between two balances. It has no debit and credit sides and is not part of double entry, so nothing is posted from it. Only items needing a cash book entry are entered in the cash book.

marking_scheme.step: Statement, not an account; no double entry
Only items needing an entry are recorded in the cash book

questions.stem_md: On 31 January 2027 Neel Traders has overdrawn its account with Sagar Bank. State how the overdraft appears in the cash book and in the pass book.
questions.solution_md: Reverse of a favourable balance in each book.

answer.model_answer_md: In the cash book the overdraft is a credit balance in the bank column. In the pass book it is a debit balance, because the bank has advanced money to the firm and is owed it.

marking_scheme.step: Credit balance in the cash book
Debit balance in the pass book

questions.stem_md: Cheques of ₹5,500 issued by Neel Traders on 28 June 2026 were presented only on 4 July. Explain how this causes a difference on 30 June and which book shows the higher balance.
questions.solution_md: Timing difference: recorded by the firm first.

answer.model_answer_md: The firm credited the bank column when it issued the cheques, but the bank debits the account only on presentation. On 30 June the cash book is therefore lower and the pass book is higher by ₹5,500, assuming favourable balances.

marking_scheme.step: Recorded by the firm on issue, by the bank on presentation
Pass book higher by the amount

questions.stem_md: Sagar Bank returned unpaid, on 27 March 2027, a cheque of ₹6,500 that Neel Traders had received from Rekha Stores and deposited. State the entry the firm must make in its cash book once it learns of this.
questions.solution_md: The receipt is reversed.

answer.model_answer_md: Credit the bank column of the cash book with ₹6,500 and debit the account of Rekha Stores with ₹6,500, so that the debt of the customer is revived.

marking_scheme.step: Debit the customer, reviving the debt

questions.stem_md: Distinguish a timing difference from an error, giving one example of each from the books of Neel Traders.
questions.solution_md: Delay against mistake.

answer.model_answer_md: A timing difference arises because one book records a transaction later than the other, as with a cheque issued but not yet presented, and it corrects itself. An error is a mistake, such as adding the bank column wrongly, and must be corrected.

questions.stem_md: Sagar Bank credited interest of ₹1,260 to the account of Neel Traders on 30 September 2026, but the firm has not entered it. State the effect on the two balances and the entry the firm must make.
questions.solution_md: Bank item: recorded by the bank first.

answer.model_answer_md: The pass book balance is higher by ₹1,260. The firm must debit the bank column of the cash book with ₹1,260, interest being a receipt.

questions.stem_md: On 31 May 2027 the accountant of Neel Traders finds six differences between the books: (i) bank charges of ₹210 debited by the bank; (ii) a cheque of ₹4,000 issued but not yet presented; (iii) a direct deposit of ₹2,500 by a customer; (iv) a cheque of ₹6,000 deposited but not yet collected; (v) a dividend of ₹1,800 collected by the bank; (vi) a premium of ₹2,200 paid by the bank on standing instruction. Say for each whether the cash book needs an entry and, if so, on which side of the bank column.
questions.solution_md: Items recorded by the firm first need no entry; items recorded by the bank first do.

answer.model_answer_md:
| Item | Treatment |
|---|---|
| Bank charges of ₹210 debited by the bank | Entry needed in the cash book (credit the bank column) |
| Cheque of ₹4,000 issued, not yet presented | No entry needed; already in the cash book |
| Direct deposit of ₹2,500 by a customer | Entry needed in the cash book (debit the bank column) |
| Cheque of ₹6,000 deposited, not yet collected | No entry needed; already in the cash book |
| Dividend of ₹1,800 collected by the bank | Entry needed in the cash book (debit the bank column) |
| Premium of ₹2,200 paid by the bank on standing instruction | Entry needed in the cash book (credit the bank column) |

marking_scheme.step: Items (ii) and (iv): no entry, already in the cash book
Items (iii) and (v): debit the bank column
Items (i) and (vi): credit the bank column

questions.stem_md: Name three causes of difference between the cash book and the pass book of Neel Traders in which the bank records the item first, and say whether each raises or lowers the pass book balance relative to the cash book.
questions.solution_md: Bank-first items and their effects.

answer.model_answer_md: Interest allowed by the bank, a direct deposit by a customer and a dividend collected by the bank each raise the pass book balance relative to the cash book. Bank charges, a payment on standing instruction and a dishonoured cheque lower it. Any three with the effect.

marking_scheme.step: Each shown as recorded by the bank first

questions.stem_md: Compare the cash book and the pass book of Neel Traders on three points: who keeps it, how a deposit is entered and how an overdraft appears.
questions.solution_md: Three points of comparison.

answer.model_answer_md: The firm keeps the cash book; the bank keeps the pass book. A deposit is a debit in the cash book but a credit in the pass book. An overdraft is a credit balance in the cash book but a debit balance in the pass book. The two books are mirror images.

questions.stem_md: Neel Traders finds three differences on 30 April 2027: (i) a cheque issued and not yet presented; (ii) the debit side of its bank column added ₹900 short; (iii) Sagar Bank wrongly credited the firm with ₹1,400 meant for another customer. Classify each as a timing difference or an error, say who made it, and state whether the pass book balance is higher or lower than the cash book balance because of it. (Balances are favourable.)
questions.solution_md: A cheque is a delay; a short addition understates the cash book, and a wrong credit overstates the pass book. Both errors make the pass book higher.

answer.model_answer_md:
| Item | Class | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| Cheque issued, not yet presented | Timing difference | Pass book higher |
| Wrong addition of the debit side of the cash book by ₹900 | Error in the cash book | Pass book higher by ₹900 |
| Bank wrongly credited ₹1,400 meant for another customer | Error by the bank | Pass book higher by ₹1,400 |

marking_scheme.step: Item (i): timing difference, pass book higher
Item (ii): error in the cash book, pass book higher by ₹900
Item (iii): error by the bank, pass book higher by ₹1,400

questions.stem_md: Explain any five causes of difference between the cash book balance and the pass book balance of a firm. For each say which book has recorded the item first.
questions.solution_md: Five causes with the book that records first.

answer.model_answer_md: Cheques issued but not yet presented are in the cash book only. Cheques deposited but not yet collected are in the cash book only. Bank charges and interest on overdraft are debited by the bank first. Interest allowed, a direct deposit by a customer and a dividend collected by the bank are credited by the bank first. A payment on standing instruction, and a deposited cheque that is dishonoured, are in the pass book first. Errors in either book are a further cause.

marking_scheme.step: Each cause correctly stated with the book that records it first (1 mark each)

questions.stem_md: Explain why a firm such as Neel Traders should prepare a bank reconciliation statement regularly. Mention the two groups into which the differences fall.
questions.solution_md: Needs and the two groups of differences.

answer.model_answer_md: The statement shows the reasons for a difference between the two balances and so checks the work of both the firm and the bank. It helps detect errors and frauds in time and shows the entries needed to update the cash book. Differences are of two kinds: timing differences, where one book records a transaction later than the other, and errors, where a mistake has been made in either book.

marking_scheme.step: Two groups: timing differences and errors

questions.stem_md: Neel Traders prepares a statement from a favourable balance in its cash book. Cheques issued but not yet presented for payment are

options.text_md: added, because the cash book has already deducted them and the bank has not
deducted, because they have not been paid by the bank
ignored, because they are timing differences
deducted, because the cash book has already deducted them

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** added, because the cash book has already deducted them and the bank has not. The cash book is lower than the pass book by these cheques, so they are added to reach the pass book balance. Deducting them would count the same payment twice, and a timing difference still has to be shown.

questions.stem_md: Starting from a favourable balance in the pass book, Neel Traders treats cheques deposited but not yet collected by the bank as

options.text_md: a deduction, because the bank has not yet credited them
an addition, because the cash book has already counted them and the bank has not
an addition, because they are credits in the pass book
not to be shown, because the bank will credit them later

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** an addition, because the cash book has already counted them and the bank has not. The cash book already includes these cheques and is therefore higher than the pass book. From the pass book the amount is added to reach the cash book balance.

questions.stem_md: On 30 June 2027 the pass book of Neel Traders shows an overdraft. Starting from this overdraft, a cheque issued but not yet presented is

options.text_md: deducted, because the cheque is a payment
added, because every payment is added to a balance
ignored, because an overdraft cannot be reconciled
added, because the cash book overdraft is larger by the amount of the cheque

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** added, because the cash book overdraft is larger by the amount of the cheque. The cash book has already recorded the payment, so its overdraft is larger than the bank's by that amount; the cheque therefore raises the overdraft and is added. The rule of adding or deducting is reversed when the start is an overdraft.

questions.stem_md: Before preparing a statement, the accountant of Neel Traders first prepares an amended cash book. Its purpose is to

options.text_md: record in the cash book the items the bank has already recorded but the firm has not, so that only the remaining timing differences are left for the statement
record cheques issued but not presented, so that the pass book can be corrected
correct the pass book using the cash book
remove all differences so that no statement is needed

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** record in the cash book the items the bank has already recorded but the firm has not, so that only the remaining timing differences are left for the statement. The amended cash book brings the firm's record up to date for bank charges, interest, direct deposits and similar items. The statement is still needed, because cheques issued and deposited but not yet cleared remain as timing differences.

questions.stem_md: After the cash book of Neel Traders has been amended, the items that normally remain in the reconciliation statement are

options.text_md: bank charges and interest on overdraft
direct deposits and dividends collected by the bank
cheques issued but not yet presented and cheques deposited but not yet collected
every difference found at the start

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** cheques issued but not yet presented and cheques deposited but not yet collected. Items the bank recorded first have now been entered in the cash book. Only items recorded by the firm first, the unpresented and uncollected cheques, still separate the balances. A bank error would also remain.

questions.stem_md: On 30 April 2027 the cash book of Neel Traders shows a favourable balance of ₹18,000. Cheques of ₹4,000 were issued but not presented, a cheque of ₹7,000 was deposited but not yet collected, and Sagar Bank charged ₹150 that the firm has not entered. The balance as per the pass book is
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** ₹14,850. Add the cheques not presented, deduct the cheque not collected and the charges: 18,000 + 4,000 − 7,000 − 150 = ₹14,850. ₹20,850 reverses the first two signs, ₹15,000 leaves out the bank charges, and ₹29,150 adds everything.

questions.stem_md: The cash book of Neel Traders shows a favourable balance of ₹6,000 on 31 May 2027. Cheques of ₹1,500 were issued but not presented, and Sagar Bank paid an insurance premium of ₹9,500 on standing instruction that the firm has not entered. The pass book balance is

options.text_md: an overdraft of ₹2,000
a favourable balance of ₹2,000
a favourable balance of ₹17,000
an overdraft of ₹14,000

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** an overdraft of ₹2,000. 6,000 + 1,500 − 9,500 = −2,000. A negative result is not a favourable balance: it is an overdraft of ₹2,000. The other options ignore the sign or add every item.

questions.stem_md: On 31 March 2027 Neel Traders finds that Sagar Bank debited its account with a cheque of ₹3,000 that was drawn by another customer. In the statement and the books of the firm this item

options.text_md: is entered in the amended cash book by crediting the bank column
is entered in the cash book by debiting the bank column
is ignored, because the bank can never make a mistake
remains in the reconciliation statement as a bank error until the bank corrects it, and the firm makes no cash book entry

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** remains in the reconciliation statement as a bank error until the bank corrects it, and the firm makes no cash book entry. The mistake is the bank's, so the firm's cash book is right and is not changed. The item stays in the statement as a reconciling item until the bank puts it right.

questions.stem_md: Neel Traders starts from a favourable balance in its pass book. A customer's cheque deposited earlier was dishonoured and debited by the bank, but the cash book still shows it as a receipt. In the statement this cheque is

options.text_md: deducted, because the bank has debited it
added, because the cash book balance is higher by the cheque
ignored, because the cheque was deposited
added to the pass book and entered in the cash book as a receipt

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** added, because the cash book balance is higher by the cheque. The cash book still counts a receipt that the bank has reversed, so it is higher than the pass book by the cheque. Starting from the pass book, the amount is added to reach the cash book figure.

questions.stem_md: Two assistants of Neel Traders prepare statements for 30 September 2026 from the same books, one starting from the cash book and the other from the pass book. Which judgement is correct?

options.text_md: Both are right: each ends at the other book's balance, and every item that is added in one statement is deducted in the other
Only the statement starting from the pass book can be right
Both are right, and each item is added in both statements
The two statements may end at different figures

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are right: each ends at the other book's balance, and every item that is added in one statement is deducted in the other. The same differences are used. Reversing the starting book reverses the direction in which each is applied, so both statements reach the opposite book's balance. Adding an item in both statements would make them disagree.

questions.stem_md: Which of the following is entered in the amended cash book of Neel Traders?

options.text_md: A cheque of ₹6,500 issued and not yet presented
Interest of ₹640 allowed by Sagar Bank and shown in the pass book
A cheque of ₹9,000 deposited and not yet collected
A mistaken credit of ₹2,000 made by the bank

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Interest of ₹640 allowed by Sagar Bank and shown in the pass book. An amended cash book takes in what the bank has recorded and the firm has not, such as interest. The two cheques are already in the cash book, and the mistaken credit is the bank's own error, which the bank must correct.

questions.stem_md: Arrange in order the steps of preparing a bank reconciliation statement.

options.text_md: Compare the cash book with the pass book entry by entry and list every difference
Check the result against the balance actually shown by the other book
Add and deduct the items to reach the balance of the other book
Decide for each difference whether it is added or deducted, from the starting book and balance
Note the balance of the book chosen as the starting point and whether it is favourable or an overdraft

questions.solution_md: **Correct order:** (e) → (a) → (d) → (c) → (b). Begin with the starting balance, find the differences, decide the sign of each, work out the result and finally check it.
